title: TDDR Rising Narratives — Wednesday morning, Nov 25
summary: A snapshot of opposition narratives from the Right and the Far Left as of 7:50 AM ET Wednesday, Nov 25, 2026. Built for TDDR (Too Dumb Didn't Read). New and on top: Kilmar Abrego Garcia's self-deportation to Spain, which DHS headlined as the exit of an 'MS-13 gang member' (a claim fact-checkers found unsupported): 22,463 posts in 24 hours, nearly all after 5 PM ET Tuesday, and on the U.S. trends list. Also new on the Right: the 'USAID Files' release, sold as proof of a Big Tech censorship machine (5,728 posts, trending as 'USAID'), and a DSA-LA board member's violent posts about Elon Musk and Sam Altman (1,379 posts, 7.32×). The 'do not certify / 38 million' query is still the largest (34,208) but cooled overnight. On the Far Left, Medicare for All posting doubled overnight (18,751) as the argument moved to a Medicare buy-in at 50; the Van Hollen push held ahead of the Dec. 1 vote (4,973). Three faded cards were dropped and three were added. Every count, quote and fact-check comes from sources and X queries pulled this morning or carried over from last evening and labeled. Nothing here is invented.

trends.detail: U.S. trends were pulled at about 7:14 AM ET with x.get_trends_by_woeid (WOEID 23424977, max 50; 50 returned). Entertainment, sports and Thanksgiving dominated: '#dwts' (109,130 posts), 'Cartagena' (126,352) and 'Miss Universe' (81,987), after Puerto Rico's Jennifer Barreto won, plus 'Good Wednesday' and 'Happy Thanksgiving Eve.' Political names included 'USAID' (45,013), 'Kilmar Abrego Garcia' (20,148), 'Mistakenly' (7,662) and 'MS-13' (6,914), which match the new USAID and Abrego Garcia cards and give both the trend bonus. 'US Army' (30,382), 'Lead Azide' (74,054) and '#IOWALeadBomb' (2,740) concerned the Army's Iowa Army Ammunition Plant detonation and are not opposition narratives. Where a trend object had no tweet_count ('#Premarket', 'ARod', 'Aaron Gordon'), its volume is unavailable and we did not estimate it.

Carried over from last evening: Democracy Docket and WOWT ('do not certify'); AL.com, FOX 7 Austin and The Advocate (Texas); AP, The National News Desk, Mediaite, The Daily Signal and Florida Daily (Newsom); CBS New York and earlier outlets (Van Hollen); Michigan Public, the Detroit Free Press and Lead Stories (audit and Michigan Wi-Fi); and Townhall and Mediaite ('fine people'). oppositionNote.body: Right = narratives the Right is pushing after the Democratic midterm wave. Far Left = pressure on Democratic leadership and the incoming majority from the party's left. The new Abrego Garcia card is tagged Right because it uses his departure to brand the Democrats who defended him, including Senate leader candidate Chris Van Hollen. The new USAID card is tagged Right because it casts a past Democratic administration's programs as a censorship operation. The new DSA-LA card is tagged Right because it uses one activist's posts to brand L.A.'s incoming Democratic socialist mayor and the party's left. The 'do not certify,' audit and Michigan Wi-Fi cards are tagged Right because they cast doubt on elections Democrats won. The Newsom card is the administration's attack on a Democratic governor. The Texas card uses an activist's speech to brand the incoming Democratic state government. The 'fine people' card uses a Fox co-host's comment to brand Democrats as liars. The Medicare for All and Van Hollen cards are tagged Far Left because they are pressure from the party's left on Democratic leaders.

methodology: Last updated Wednesday, Nov 25, 2026, 7:50 AM ET. This is a research snapshot for TDDR, not a live API, and it will go stale. U.S. X trends were pulled at about 7:14 AM ET. Last evening's snapshot (Nov 24, 5:20 PM ET) is kept in the archive and was not overwritten. Eight of its eleven narratives were re-counted with the same queries so momentum compares like with like. The new 24-hour window overlaps last evening's by 10 hours (7 AM to 5 PM ET Tuesday), so each carried card also reports its overnight count (5 PM Tuesday to 7 AM Wednesday ET) against the same hours a night earlier. Three narratives were dropped because they faded: the Rikers card (3,505 posts in the last 24 hours, 0.26× its prior daily average; last evening 5,799); the Somali–Minnesota card (3,149 posts in the last 24 hours, 0.25× its prior daily average; last evening 4,847); the 'Democrats will raise your taxes' card (731 posts in the last 24 hours, 0.32× its prior daily average; last evening 1,843). Three were added with new queries: Abrego Garcia, the USAID Files and the DSA-LA board member. Other candidates were counted and not carved out as cards: Mayor Mamdani's ICE hotline and his chief counsel pick (2,442 posts, 1.32×), the backlash to the DSCC backing Sen. John Fetterman (236 posts, 0.92×), and Republican claims that Democrats risk a Dec. 11 shutdown over Iran war funding (54 posts with our query).

For each narrative we ran one English-language X search with x.get_posts_counts_recent twice: at daily granularity over a 167-hour window from 8:00 AM ET Wednesday, Nov 18, through 7:00 AM ET Wednesday, Nov 25 (the 'seven-day' total), and at hourly granularity from 7:00 AM ET Tuesday, Nov 24, through 7:00 AM ET Wednesday, Nov 25 (the 24-hour count). We counted named news or fact-check outlets whose coverage we opened or retrieved and cite on the card. Official government pages, congressional records, advocacy groups, blogs, X News summaries and X posts are cited as sources but not counted as outlets; this morning that includes DHS, Congress.gov and Unite4Freedom. This morning we researched the three new cards and re-researched the 'do not certify' and Medicare for All cards; the audit, Van Hollen and Newsom cards add X News items but carry last evening's outlet counts, and the Michigan Wi-Fi, Texas and 'fine people' cards carry last evening's research and say so. 'Kilmar Abrego Garcia,' 'MS-13' and 'USAID' were on the U.S. trends list at about 7:14 AM ET.

Score = 50% volume index + 30% acceleration index + 20% coverage index. Volume index is 100 × log10(1 + last-24h posts) / log10(1 + the highest last-24h count in this set). Acceleration index is 100 × min(last-24h / prior daily average, 3) / 3, so a triple-or-higher average scores 100. Prior daily average is (seven-day total − last 24h) / 6. Coverage index is 70 × min(outlets, 7) / 7, plus 30 if the topic was on the U.S. X trends list when we pulled it. The Abrego Garcia and USAID queries had near-zero baselines before Tuesday, so their acceleration indexes are maxed out and their multiples (hundreds of times) mean 'new,' not 'hundreds of times bigger.' The volume ceiling this morning is 34,208 (the 'do not certify' query), down from 47,441 last evening, which raises every other card's volume index. Read the post counts alongside the scores.

Counts are query matches, not unique posts or unique users, and queries can overlap. The Abrego Garcia query matches his name, so it catches straight news relays and his defenders. The USAID query requires USAID plus a censorship, GDI, Big Tech or content-moderation term, so it catches rebuttals. The DSA query requires DSA or 'Democratic Socialists' plus Musk, Altman, RFK or a violence term, so it catches unrelated posts about DSA and violence. The other queries are unchanged from last evening and carry the same caveats: the 'do not certify' query catches rebuttals and other countries' elections; the Medicare for All query catches supporters, opponents and unrelated 'M4A' uses; the Van Hollen query catches syndicated news. Replies are included. Sentiment is a qualitative label from relevancy-sorted post samples and from quotes in news coverage, not a scientific poll. This morning we pulled fresh samples for the Abrego Garcia, USAID, DSA-LA, 'do not certify' and Medicare for All queries; the other cards carry last evening's sentiment and say so. disinfo.caveatBody: New this morning: 'Abrego Garcia is an MS-13 gang member' is not supported. Fact-checkers found the claim rested on a 2019 informant's account and his clothing, and that he had no criminal conviction (PolitiFact; USA Today; Snopes, 2025); DHS's Nov. 24 release repeats the label without new evidence that we found. 'The USAID Files prove the government censored Americans' goes beyond what we could verify: the released files are real and include a 2022 GDI concept note proposing a partnership and describing an ad-tech exclusion list used by advertisers (The Boston Report), but we found no rated fact-check and did not review the 248 files ourselves. '38 million invalid voters' is still not a finding of illegal votes: Unite4Freedom's own scorecard describes 'registrations prohibited by law' by its own analysis (Unite4Freedom), and Alaska certified its results and the Republican incumbent conceded (X News). Carried over from last evening: '38 million invalid voters, so the midterms can't be certified' misstates its own source. The figure comes from the group Unite4Freedom via Joe Hoft's blog, and Unite4Freedom describes the 38 million as 'registrations flagged for further investigation – not 38 million proven illegal registrations.' A flagged roll record (a move, a death, a data mismatch) is not a ballot cast illegally, and we found no official finding that any state's result is in doubt; Iowa's Republican secretary of state defended his state's results (WOWT), and leading 2020 election deniers including Cleta Mitchell and Michael Flynn accepted this year's results (Democracy Docket). We found no rated fact-check of the 38 million figure itself. 'Texas Democrats say the T stands for trans' turns one activist's gala speech into the incoming government's position; she said 'is for trans,' and the 'stands for' wording came from repost captions (The Watering Hole). 'Newsom is letting killers go free' is false. The commutations would change 548 death sentences to life without the possibility of parole, and none has taken effect: the California Constitution requires the state Supreme Court to approve clemency for anyone with more than one felony conviction, and Newsom's office says it will wait for the court (The National News Desk). Trump's earlier figure of '563' death-row inmates does not match the 548 in the commutation; his new memorandum applies to federal cases and federal death sentences, not California's state death row (White House; AP). The Michigan Wi-Fi claim still has no official finding behind it: the voting system's federal certificate lists no wireless LAN or WAN (U.S. Election Assistance Commission), we found no reported result from the sheriff or CISA, and the bipartisan Board of State Canvassers certified Michigan's results on Nov. 23 (Michigan Department of State; Michigan Public).

Leaving after a year of detention threats is not a confession; his lawyers say it is temporary. The point of the fight was due process for everyone, and a government that can wrongly ship one person to a foreign prison can do it to anyone.

Bernie Sanders and Jeff Merkley and Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan. Reporters and aggregators: @jsolomonReports, @JustTheNews, @CraigCaplan, @LauraEWeiss16, @TIME. On the other side, Schumer's backers include Sen. Angela Alsobrooks.
narratives.whyItWorks: Each new endorsement is a fresh, concrete news peg in a race with a date, a vote count (28) and a clear villain for the left: a 76-year-old leader who has led Democrats since 2017. Slotkin is a moderate, so her backing lets the left argue the challenge is mainstream, not fringe. The filibuster clip gives supporters a simple promise to share.
narratives.audience: Progressive and younger Democrats, Sanders and El-Sayed voters, activists who blame Schumer for past compromises, and political-insider audiences following the whip count.
narratives.counter: Treat it as a normal leadership race, not a crisis: the caucus votes by secret ballot on Dec. 1 and most senators have not declared (The Washington Post; The Hill). Keep the focus on the agenda both candidates say they want, lower costs and a faster Senate, and note that Van Hollen himself says rules changes are the caucus's call (Roll Call).

talkingPoints: Even Fox's resident liberal admits it: Trump never called neo-Nazis 'very fine people.'
Biden launched his 2020 campaign on the 'fine people' hoax.
The media chopped off 'I'm not talking about the neo-Nazis' and Democrats ran on the edited clip for nine years.
Millions of voters still believe it, and that's how Democrats win.
narratives.amplifiers: Right: @EricLDaugh (810,352 views), @clerpatriot, @DKH013, @Bubblebathgirl, PJ Media, Gateway Pundit and Twitchy (via news aggregators), and pro-Trump aggregator sites. 'Jessica Tarlov' was a U.S. X trend Monday morning.
narratives.whyItWorks: It packages a years-old argument as fresh news with a confession from the other side, which is the most shareable format in partisan media. The kernel is real: Trump did say he was 'not talking about the neo-Nazis and the white nationalists,' and Snopes rated the claim that he called them 'very fine people' False. That lets the Right generalize from one overstated line to 'Democrats lie about everything' right as the new majority starts making promises.
narratives.audience: Trump voters and Fox viewers who have long called the line a hoax; independents who remember the 2017 clip but not the full quote; and media-skeptical younger men who share 'gotcha' clips.
narratives.counter: Don't relitigate the clip. Concede the precise point — he excluded neo-Nazis by name — and add what fact-checkers said alongside it: Snopes notes that virtually every account found the rally was organized and attended by white supremacists, so 'very fine people on both sides' was itself wrong. Then move on: a nine-year-old quote fight is a distraction from prices, health care and what the new Congress will do.

factChecks.claim: Trump called the neo-Nazis and white supremacists at the 2017 Charlottesville rally 'very fine people.'
factChecks.detail: Trump said there were 'very fine people on both sides' but, in the same answer, said he was 'not talking about the neo-Nazis and the white nationalists, because they should be condemned totally.' Snopes's editor's note adds that virtually every source found the rally was conceived, led and attended by white supremacists, so the 'both sides' characterization was itself wrong.
